text: The Quantum Fourier Transform doesn't do anything useful on its own — it's the engine inside phase estimation, and phase estimation is the engine inside Shor's algorithm and quantum chemistry simulation. Knowing how it looks as a Q# building block matters because you'll be calling it, not reinventing it, almost every time.

Four things to hold onto: the QFT maps a computational basis state to a superposition over every basis state, with a phase on each term that depends on the input and output index — the quantum analogue of the discrete Fourier transform. It's a change of basis, not an answer by itself. Q#'s standard libraries ship a built-in ApplyQFT operation, so you essentially never hand-roll it for real work. And a verified exact calculation shows exactly what it produces for a small concrete input.

The formula says QFT turns |j> into a sum over every |k>, weighted by a complex phase depending on j and k — that's precisely what phase estimation needs: a way to turn a phase you can't directly measure into a bitstring you can. In practice, you just open the Canon library and call ApplyQFT on your qubit register, which takes care of exactly how the Hadamards and controlled-phase rotations get ordered — easy to get backwards by hand and hard to debug if you do.

If you did write it yourself, the QFT on an n-qubit register is a Hadamard on the first qubit, followed by controlled-phase rotations between it and every other qubit, recursively the same pattern on the rest, finished with a reversal of qubit order. Walking through this isn't to suggest you should write it this way in practice — it's that the controlled-phase angles here are exactly where the Fourier phases in the formula come from, gate by gate.

For a 2-qubit register starting in |01>, the formula was evaluated exactly with explicit complex-number arithmetic. Every one of the four output amplitudes has magnitude exactly 0.5, so each basis state is measured with probability exactly 0.25 — and the phases step by ninety degrees per output index. Every output is equally likely to be measured; the information isn't in which basis state you get, it's in the relative phases between them, which is exactly why QFT output is almost never measured directly on its own.

Next lesson moves to a third building block: quantum teleportation, which moves a qubit's exact state to another qubit using entanglement and two classical bits — no physical qubit travels, and nothing travels faster than light.
